performers: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, baritone; Berlin Philharmonic; Rudolf Kempe, conductor
intro: A father rages at the weather, then sings his children to sleep. Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, Rudolf Kempe and the Berlin Philharmonic close Kindertotenlieder with a storm that leaves behind a celesta and a lullaby.

sections.label: A · The father in the storm
sections.mNote: Restless winds, trembling cellos and sharp harp chords

sections.label: Link · Piccolo and small bell
sections.mNote: The storm slows around a held high note

sections.label: B · A D-major lullaby
sections.mNote: Celesta and quiet strings rock beneath the baritone

sections.label: Coda · Horns after the voice
sections.mNote: Bassoon and horns sing above the rocking violas

cues.title: The storm starts quietly
cues.text: The winds dart in short phrases, cellos tremble, and the harp strikes accented chords. Much of this storm begins softly. Mahler asks for “ruhelos schmerzvollem Ausdruck” — restless, painful expression — before Fischer-Dieskau has sung a word.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), p. 60: Mit ruhelos schmerzvollem Ausdruck and the opening dynamics; our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Carried out of the house
cues.text: Rückert’s father keeps saying he would never send his children out in such weather. Then comes the unbearable correction: “man hat sie getragen hinaus” — they were carried out. “Ich durfte nichts dazu sagen” — I was allowed no say in it.
cues.evidence: Rückert, In diesem Wetter, first stanza as set by Mahler; German text at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindertotenlieder#Text. Our translations.

cues.title: A piccolo above the storm
cues.text: A high piccolo note and the small bell remain as the storm loses speed. String phrases fall away in shorter waves. Mahler writes “Allmählich langsamer” — gradually slower — across the bridge into the final stanza.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 78–79, rehearsal 8: piccolo, Glöckchen and Allmählich langsamer; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The father sings a lullaby
cues.text: “Langsam. Wie ein Wiegenlied” — slow, like a lullaby. Fischer-Dieskau sings the weather words again, now over celesta and rocking strings in D major. The children rest “als wie in der Mutter Haus” — as in their mother’s house.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 79–84: lullaby marking, two-sharp signature and Rückert’s final stanza. Our translations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The cradle keeps rocking
cues.text: The baritone finishes on the mother’s house. The violas keep rocking; bassoon and horns begin their own soft phrases above divided cellos. Mahler lets the orchestra stay with the sleeping children after the parent falls silent.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 84–85, rehearsal 10: voice ends on Haus; rocking violas, bassoon, horns and divided cellos.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: D major, almost gone
cues.text: The celesta’s little figures descend through the last bars. Low strings, horns and clarinets settle into D major, with the final chord marked as softly as the instruments can sustain it. The cycle that began before sunrise ends here.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 86: Morendo dim., celesta gänzlich verklingend, final D-major chord at ppp. The existing late cue marks the closing passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A high D survives the storm
transitions.from: A · The father in the storm
transitions.how: At rehearsal 8 a high D in the piccolo hangs above the retreating orchestra. The small bell repeats its notes, with harp chords and low bassoon underneath. Allmählich langsamer slows the falling string phrases until the D-minor storm has almost emptied out.

transitions.title: D minor turns to D major
transitions.how: The piccolo holds across the change to a two-sharp key signature. D minor becomes D major. Celesta and soft strings take up the rocking figure under Langsam. Wie ein Wiegenlied; the low strings leave space around the singer’s quiet return.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 79, transition into the last stanza. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425

transitions.title: The violas continue after “Haus”
transitions.how: The voice ends on “Haus” while the violas continue their rocking figure. Divided cellos sustain the bass; horn and bassoon lines enter above, marked weich — soft. The D-major postlude continues the lullaby without a pause.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 84, rehearsal 10, through p. 86. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song V, printed pp. 60–86: storm music, the high piccolo and small bell, then the D-major lullaby with celesta.

timeline.note: Opening storm: short wind figures, muted strings, tremolo cellos and accented harp chords.
The baritone’s protests cut across the short wind phrases and restless strings.
A held high piccolo note and the small bell remain as the storm subsides.
Celesta and soft strings accompany the lullaby; the bass line falls silent at its opening.
Horn and bassoon continue after the voice, with rocking violas and divided cellos.
The celesta descends while winds and strings settle into the final D-major chord.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
